Chapter 3: Stereotypes and Survival — The Burden of Misrepresentation
Every day, Black women move through a world shaped by assumptions—assumptions that aren’t just simple misunderstandings.
These are powerful stories, the kind that shape not only how others see them, but sometimes, how they see themselves. The legacy of slavery left behind a set of stubborn images and ideas that refuse to fade away.
One of the most damaging? It’s the idea that Black women are naturally strong—able to endure anything, no matter what, without ever complaining. On the surface, that might sound like a compliment, right? But really, it’s a way of denying their pain.
If a woman’s always expected to be tough, her suffering gets ignored. She’s told to keep pushing through, even when she’s hurting inside.
Then, there’s the old “jezebel” stereotype—the image of a woman seen as sexually aggressive, or somehow immoral. This idea has been used to excuse everything from workplace harassment to actual violence. It’s a way of blaming Black women for the mistreatment they experience, instead of holding others responsible.
And let’s not forget the “mammy”—the loyal, self-sacrificing caretaker who always puts everyone else first. That image might be comforting for those who benefit from her labor, but where does it leave her? She’s expected to give and give, never asking for anything in return. Her own dreams and desires end up pushed aside.
What’s tough is that these stereotypes don’t just come from outside. Over time, they can sneak into the way Black women see themselves.
Imagine a young woman who feels like she has to hide her vulnerability—afraid that showing any weakness will just confirm someone’s low expectations. Or another, who struggles to set boundaries because she’s worried she’ll be labeled as angry or difficult.
Most of the time, people don’t even notice how these images shape everyday life. They have a say in who gets hired, who gets promoted, and who’s believed when they speak up about injustice. They affect friendships, relationships, even how people parent their children.
And yet, even with all these challenges, Black women keep finding ways to survive and resist. Some turn to art—music, poetry, dance—to tell their own stories, in their own voices. Others build tight networks of support, leaning on friends and family when the world feels harsh.
Sometimes, resistance looks like small acts of defiance: Speaking up at work, setting healthy boundaries, or just refusing to let anyone else define who they are. In these moments, they reclaim their full humanity.
What’s become clear is that breaking free from these stereotypes is about more than just individual strength. It’s about changing the stories that society tells about Black women—and making space for their whole, complicated selves.
